section.title: Signed area and net change
section.p: The definite integral was built from Riemann sums:
Each term has two parts. The width \Delta x_j is positive when we move from left to right. The height f(x_j^*) can be positive, zero, or negative.
That one fact changes the meaning of area.

If the graph lies above the x-axis, the rectangles contribute positively. If the graph lies below the x-axis, the rectangles contribute negatively. So the definite integral is not ordinary area first. It is signed accumulation.
section.md: \int_a^b f(x)\,dx = \text{area above the axis} - \text{area below the axis}.
section.p: Ordinary area is never negative. A definite integral can be negative, because it is designed to remember direction.

exercise.title: Why is a definite integral signed accumulation rather than ordinary area?

statement.p: In a Riemann sum the widths are positive when we move left to right, but the heights can be negative. In your own words, why does that make the integral equal to area above the axis minus area below, and why can an integral be negative when ordinary area cannot?

hint.p: Ordinary area is never negative. A definite integral is designed to remember direction, just as velocity remembers forward and backward motion.

subsection.title: Cancellation and meaning
subsection.p: Signed area can cancel.
For example, consider
on [-1,1]. The graph lies below the axis on [-1,0] and above the axis on [0,1]. The two triangles have the same ordinary area:
The signed integral is
But the graph is not zero. The function does not vanish. The integral is zero because the negative and positive contributions balance exactly.

note.title: An integral can be zero for two different reasons
note.p: It may be zero because there is no accumulation.
It may also be zero because positive and negative accumulation cancel.

subsection.p: This distinction is crucial in motion.
If a car travels 40 miles east and then 40 miles west, its displacement is 0. But it did not stay still. It traveled 80 miles.
The signed integral measures net change. It does not measure total activity.

exercise.title: Why can an integral be zero for two different reasons?

statement.p: The integral of x from -1 to 1 is zero, even though the graph is not the zero function. In your own words, why might an integral vanish because nothing accumulated, and why might it vanish because positive and negative accumulation cancelled?

hint.p: A car that travels forty miles east and forty miles west has displacement zero, but it did not stay still. The signed integral measures net change, not total activity.

exercise.title: Why does integrating velocity give displacement, while integrating speed gives distance?

statement.p: \int_a^b v(t)\,dt is net change in position. \int_a^b |v(t)|\,dt is total distance traveled. In your own words, why does the absolute value remove cancellation, and why must we always ask what the sign of the integrand means?

hint.p: Net signed accumulation is positive contributions minus negative ones. Total accumulation is the same two contributions added.

The definite integral is therefore more flexible than ordinary area. It can measure area, displacement, accumulated signed change, or cancellation. To use it well, we must always ask what the sign means.
The next section collects the algebraic rules that make integrals useful. These rules will look familiar because they come from the same place as the integral itself: finite sums.

exercise.title: Why is net change no substitute for total change?

statement.p: The two formulas \int_a^b f and \int_a^b |f| answer different questions. In your own words, why can the total be strictly larger than the absolute value of the net, and what does that difference tell you about cancellation along the way?

hint.p: Cancellation is removed when we integrate the absolute value. The total is larger precisely when the graph spent time on both sides of the axis.
